criterion_notes.c1: The paper focuses on piped drinking water supply and sewage collection and treatment coverage in Brazil, addressing gaps in household/population access and the 2033 universalization goals.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both readings of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it directly examines legal, regulatory, and institutional factors (Law 11.445/2007, Law 14.026/2020, subnational regulatory fragmentation, and ANA's mandate). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it addresses utility ownership and regulatory structure rules governing service provision—specifically ending unbid public/public program contracts, mandating competitive bidding for concessions, inserting mandatory universalization targets into contracts, and conditioning federal funding on municipal regionalization and adoption of ANA standard guidelines—alongside broader macro-regulatory governance. However, both plain and narrow readings still result in exclusion due to lack of empirical evidence (Criterion 3, E05).
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). This is a descriptive legal and policy overview / doctrinal commentary written shortly after the July 2020 enactment of Law 14.026/2020. It has no empirical study design, no primary data collection, no empirical analysis linking legal/regulatory variation to service access, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; secondary descriptive tables (e.g., SNIS coverage, Giambiagi sector investment, Juliatto agency counts) are cited solely as contextual background for prospective commentary.
criterion_notes.c4: No empirical access outcome of the focal legal reform is measured or reported. While pre-reform regional water supply and sanitation coverage rates from SNIS (2018-2019) are cited descriptively as background context, the discussion of Law 14.026/2020's impact on service coverage consists solely of prospective author predictions regarding whether 2033 universalization goals will be met.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, and empirical exposure-outcome measurement, as the article is a narrative legal-policy commentary rather than an empirical study.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, which is an eligible language without translation.

study_design: Non-empirical legal and policy overview / doctrinal commentary (no empirical study design reported)
population_and_sample: National WSS sector in Brazil (descriptive secondary background figures cited for up to 5,570 municipalities and 202.2 million inhabitants; no empirical study sample)
exposure: Law 14.026/2020 (2020 reform of Brazil's water and sanitation legal and regulatory framework, including ANA standard regulatory guidelines, regionalization, contract standardization, and mandatory competitive bidding)
outcome: Prospective commentary on achievement of universalization goals for drinking water supply and sewage collection and treatment coverage (descriptive pre-reform SNIS coverage statistics cited only as background; no empirical outcome measured)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper addresses water and sanitation service access in Brazil (c1) and examines the legal, contractual, utility-ownership, and regulatory provisions of Law 14.026/2020 (c2), it is a non-empirical legal and policy commentary that describes the historical institutional background, summarizes the newly enacted July 2020 statute, and offers prospective author opinions on future implementation challenges without any empirical methodology, primary data, or systematic empirical synthesis (c3 = no). Both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2 yield exclusion on E05 grounds.
